title: Section 49 Registration Act — Effect of non-registration

content.overview: An unregistered document required to be registered under section 17 or the Transfer of Property Act cannot affect immovable property, confer a power to adopt, or be received as evidence of the transaction, subject to a limited proviso.
content.study: Section 49 is the enforcement tooth of compulsory registration. The proviso still allows the unregistered instrument as evidence of a contract in a specific-performance suit, or of a collateral transaction not required to be effected by registered instrument. Link to TPA section 54 and SRA specific performance.

learningObjectives: Explain Registration Act, 1908 Section 49 and its role in the registration scheme.
Apply the section to a factual document without confusing compulsory and optional registration.
Connect the provision with related statutory consequences where applicable.
enhancement.definition: Section 49 sets out the principal consequences of failing to register a document that the Registration Act or the Transfer of Property Act requires to be registered, while preserving limited uses under its proviso.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Non-registration prevents the document from producing the statutory effects specified in Section 49, but the proviso preserves limited evidentiary uses such as a contract in a specific-performance suit and qualifying collateral transactions.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Registration Act, 1908, Section 49 and its proviso; read with Section 17 and applicable Transfer of Property Act registration requirements.
essentialIngredients: The document must be one that the law requires to be registered.
Apply the statutory disabilities: affecting immovable property, conferring a power to adopt, or being received as evidence of the transaction, as applicable.
Then test the proviso for specific performance or a qualifying collateral transaction.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 49 is best understood as the consequence provision linked to compulsory registration. The main rule denies specified legal effects to an unregistered document that required registration. The proviso does not generally validate the unregistered transaction; it creates limited evidentiary uses. The Supreme Court has emphasized that an unregistered document cannot be used to confer title, while recognizing the statutory proviso for specific-performance and collateral purposes.
examples: If an unregistered sale document is required to be registered, it cannot itself transfer title to the immovable property. Depending on the facts, it may nevertheless be considered for a contract in a specific-performance suit or a qualifying collateral transaction under the proviso.
enhancement.distinctions: The main part of Section 49 concerns the disabilities caused by non-registration; the proviso creates limited exceptions. Section 17 determines whether compulsory registration is required in the first place.

caseLaw.name: Shakeel Ahmed v. Syed Akhlaq Hussain
caseLaw.holding: The Supreme Court held that compulsory registration requirements arise from statute and that an unregistered agreement to sell or power of attorney could not confer title to immovable property.
caseLaw.relevance: Direct authority on the effect of Sections 17 and 49 on unregistered documents affecting immovable property.

caseLaw.name: R. Hemalatha v. Kashthuri
caseLaw.holding: The Supreme Court reiterated that an unregistered document required to be registered is inadmissible to prove the transaction requiring registration, while recognizing the statutory proviso for specific-performance contracts and qualifying collateral purposes.
caseLaw.relevance: Direct authority on the evidentiary operation of Section 49 and its proviso.

enhancement.problemApplication: An unregistered agreement is tendered in a specific-performance suit. First determine whether registration was required; then apply the main part of Section 49 and finally test whether the proviso permits the document to be received for the pleaded purpose.
